text: VO: With the explosive growth of massive data centers across the country, many Americans are convinced that artificial intelligence, and the infrastructure needed to run it, are what’s to blame for rising electric bills. And in some places, that’s true! But while Idaho doesn’t have the same caliber of data center incentives that a state like Virgina has, it’s still an appealing location to build a new data center – both for the relatively low cost of electricity, and for the state’s friendly business climate. JIM Buie: ‘The reliability, predictability, and just the pragmatic business climate. | Idaho checks those boxes from a business perspective. It happens to have favorable environmental conditions as well.’ VO: Data center company Valor C3 provides services to mid-tier businesses that have outgrown an internal server room but don’t need a full data facility of their own. CEO Jim Buie said Valor C3 appreciates the community, just as much as – if not more than – the low cost of power. Buie: ‘In the Idaho Power scheme, we’re a typical industrial medium scale business. Similar to a process plant. Similar to a factory… VO: Since Idaho Reports visited in November, the facility is expanding even more. The second building Valor 3C is constructing, near the existing site, hasn’t even opened yet, and BOISE DEV reports the company has already applied to build an expansion. Buie: So it’s a 5MW data center build currently. The project can expand to another 5MW which would be 10MW in total. VO: But Valor C3 is still small potatoes compared to Meta, who is planning with Idaho Power to install hundreds of MWs of solar power generation in Ada County to help power its Kuna data center. The new “Gemstone” technology park being planning right next door to the Meta site is expected to consume something like 600 to 800 MW. ANDREW Mickelsen: ‘That’s something that has us very worried. What we’ve seen is a lot of data centers looking at Idaho. Or even big manufacturing such as micron looking at Idaho and saying hey, this could be great place to go to.’ VO: Andrew Mickelsen is a potato farmer, and the son of state Rep. Stephanie Mickelsen. She’s been a leading Republican voice at the statehouse about the need to regulate data centers. STEPHANIE Mickelsen: Because of the way the PUC subsidizes rates | How are you going to tell grandma it’s okay on a fixed limited income that she’s going to subsidize the next major AI plant somewhere. ANDREW Mickelsen: It is great to see business coming to the state and we do want to encourage that growth. | But at the same time, should that cost be borne by everybody else? | Us as farmers, we’ve been here – the power usage has been here for the last 50 years. Why are we having to pay more all of a sudden. VO: Idaho Power is proud of the fact that its rates are competitive, especially compared to other parts of the country. Executive Vice President Adam Richins told Idaho Reports that reliable service, and keeping rates from rising too quickly, are the company’s top priorities. Richins: “Over the last, 15 years, our rates have average gone up 1.2% a year. That's quite a bit less than inflation. Now, we don't love that 1.2%. It's something we're trying not to do. But when you look at CPI compared to that it's still pretty low. And our generally are 20 to 30% below the national average.” VO: But local power bills are still rising, which has electric customers worried. Richins: “This last year we did have a rate increase, it ended up being settled at about 7% so that maybe what some folks are talking about. That rate case did not have any dollars related to large load infrastructure because they pay for that all upfront” |“Idaho has been very strict on this mantra of growth pays for growth. So if you’re going to come for our service territory, that’s great. We have really low rates. You need to pay your way to make sure those costs aren’t spread to other customers. VO: Idaho Power may be a big shareholder-owned company, but it deals with INFLATION just like any one of its human customers. Richins: “Inflation generally has been significant. In the energy business it has been outrageous. | Poles. Transformers. The things you see out in the world. They’re all at least twice as expensive as they were 5 years ago. Some are 300% more some are 400% more. VO: So as costs increase, Idaho has a system to oversee how quickly utilities, like Idaho Power, can increase rates. They operate as “regulated monopolies” under the Public Utilities Commission, which reviews contracts and agreements, in a mostly public fashion. Richins: It’s a public process. Any party that wants to intervene that has representation can intervene. Mickelsen: Every time we look at a rate increase, they do all these studies and they come in and say this group is costing this much, this group is costing this much. So then they propose increases based on that. Richins: “So it’s not necessarily the irrigators or… of what the rates should be.” VO: Lawmakers continued negotiating this year on whether to regulate new large load users (like data centers) tighter than the existing Public Utilities Commission processes. Richins “You see legislation coming in other states because they don't’ have this no harm process. Idaho does have it. | So why interfere with that. It’s been really successful so far | Our rates are the lowest in the nation in Idaho. These processes has been a part of that so let's keep them in place and rely on them as we move forward.” VO: House Bill 911 was delivered to the Governor’s Office on Wednesday. __________________________________________________ VO: [House Bill 911 (2026)] --- THE VOID ___ VO: Rather than create an entirely parallel review process or tie the hands of the Public Utilities Commission, the Senate proposed codifying current practices. The House wants a no-harm test as part of the process, requiring the PUC to consider whether existing customers’ bills and service reliability will stay the as they would have without the new large load user. VO: The House overwhelmingly passed a compromise bill two weeks ago, which splits the difference between the other bills. If passed in to law, the Public Utilities Commission would review new large load service contracts – defined at the widest threshold yet in this bill, a facility using 50MW over 5 years – to ensure the public utility is reasonably expected to maintain existing service, and that the new load is responsible for its full cost of service.
